name: Shoshone, Gosiute
confidence_why: one confirmed first-hand source; 5 other works read were silent
catalog_quote: Miller describes the basic stress pattern as alternating, with primary stress on the initial syllable, and an apparently optional pattern of clash tolerance by stressing the final syllable (19a–c). (19) a. "kin.ka 'onion' 12 b. "hi.pik.ka 'drank' 102 c. "nim.mi.man.tin 'one of us' 1022 (Miller 1996:698) ... Unstressed vowels in the final syllable are devoiced (Miller 1996:697–698).

audit.recode_to: Keep classification fixed-strict, dom=initial (all sources agree on initial/first-mora primary stress with left-to-right alternation). Pending Miller 1996:698 / McLaughlin 2012:11: mark the final-syllable secondary stress as OPTIONAL rather than strict (rule 101(1), 10101(1)..), note count unit = mora (Kim 1968:21; Gordon 2002 fn. 39; McLaughlin 2012), and soften the 'contra' against StressTyp2 ('every source keeps the clash') to a caution, since van Urk's relay says 'apparently optional' and Kim 1968:24 transcribes four-mora words with an unstressed final mora.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.deciding_source_kind: database or survey citing another work
audit.deciding_source_year: 1996 (Miller, relayed by Gordon 2002, StressTyp2 2015, van Urk ms.)
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the operative quotation (the domain quotation) is verbatim in the held van Urk ms. at sec. 2.2.2; StressTyp2 prose and Gordon 2002 appendix also confirmed in copies we hold. But all three are relays of Miller 1996:697-698, which we do not hold. (2) Deciding source is therefore second-hand (database/survey/ms) resting on a 1996 handbook sketch; better primary descriptions exist (McLaughlin 2012 grammar; Crum & Dayley 1993 295-pp reference grammar; Miller 1972; Elzinga 1999 Gosiute diss. (3) The held primary source Kim 1968 (MA thesis, pp. 21-25, read as page images) confirms initial primary stress and odd-mora alternation but shows even-length (four-mora) words with a weak final mora, i.e. no obligatory final clash stress; van Urk himself calls the final stress 'appa
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again: confirmed in the copy we hold, second-hand., extracted text(sec. 2.2.2 'Gosiute Shoshone'): 'Miller describes the basic stress pattern as alternating, with primary stress on the initial syllable, and an apparently optional pattern of clash tolerance by stressing the final syllable (19a-c). (19) a. "kin.ka 'onion' 12, b. "hi.pik.ka 'drank' 102, c. "nim.mi.man.tin 'one of us' 1022 (Miller 1996:698).. Although Miller does not provide a great deal of data.. Unstressed vowels in the final syllable are devoiced (Miller 1996:697-698)' — verbatim as the record's the domain quotation. van
